title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
Otter.ai's transcription service records meetings on Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams with the stated purpose of transcribing them. According to a federal lawsuit, the service collects audio data by default and uses it to train AI systems without adequately notifying meeting participants of this practice, in violation of state and federal privacy and wiretap laws. The suit alleges that while Otter's privacy policy includes a checkbox for consent to use transcripts for AI training, many users are misled about this data collection and use.

The failure is deployment without adequate human review of consent mechanisms and notification practices before widespread use. A system that records private conversations for training purposes requires clear, affirmative notice to all participants before recording begins, not a checkbox buried in a privacy policy that users may not see or understand. Catching this would have required reviewing whether users whose conversations were recorded actually understood and agreed that their audio would be used to improve Otter's models.

It is not established whether Otter's de-identification process is or is not effective, whether users actually saw or understood the checkbox in the privacy policy, or what the court will ultimately decide about the company's liability.

summary:
A federal lawsuit filed in California accuses Otter.ai, a Mountain View-based artificial intelligence company, of secretly recording private work conversations without permission. The suit claims that Otter's transcription service, which records Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams meetings, collects audio data by default without notifying meeting participants that their conversations will be used to train the company's AI systems. Plaintiff Justin Brewer alleges his privacy was violated when he discovered Otter had recorded a confidential conversation. The lawsuit contends the company violates state and federal privacy and wiretap laws and profits from this unauthorized data collection.

The case highlights growing privacy concerns as Otter's service has expanded to approximately 25 million users worldwide who have recorded over 1 billion meetings since 2016. While Otter's privacy policy states it receives explicit permission through a checkbox for using transcripts for AI training, the lawsuit maintains many users are being misled. Past incidents include an investor meeting recording that exposed sensitive business details and concerns from a journalist interviewing a human rights activist about potential Chinese government access. Otter claims it de-identifies data before using it for machine learning, though the lawsuit questions the effectiveness of this process.
